cells.tense: You're the one at the wheel right now, and the choosing is deliberate.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're steering this week and say the direction out loud to one person before it's finished — so someone else can stand beside the choice and answer it.
cells.sheetLine: The direction you're setting now holds, and you can say it while it's still moving.
cells.core:
You can hold a thing long enough to check it against what you actually want, and then commit to it out loud. The pause before you speak isn't doubt — it's the checking, and a choice that comes through it keeps its shape when the day pushes on it. This works because the deciding is yours, and you're not asking anyone to validate it first.

What this can grow into is letting one person watch the direction land while it's still in motion. Someone standing beside an unfinished choice can steer alongside you, and you find out what the direction is worth when it has room to be answered instead of delivered.

cells.place: the place where the direction gets picked

cells.tense: You're already living in how this will land, and the landing hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Write two lists this week: the decisions you're actually making, and the outcomes you're bracing for that aren't yours to decide. Underline one on the first list and do it before Friday.
cells.sheetLine: The picturing has taken over from the deciding.
cells.core:
This works when you pick a direction and stay with it after the night gets long — the picture of the outcome doesn't have to be finished before you commit, and you follow the thing you chose rather than the thing you can picture.

Right now you've pictured how it lands, how it's received, what it means three moves out — and the picturing has become the deciding. Conviction doesn't arrive that way; it gets buried under versions, and the versions don't survive contact with the week. Write the two lists. The one you're actually making this week is short; the one you're carrying for other people is long. Underline one on the short list, and do it small before Friday.

cells.tense: You knew where this was going once, and you've stopped standing in that room.
cells.ask: Take one decision you've been circling — small and real — and say it to one person, along with what following it would require of you.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped moving on a direction you'd picked.
cells.core:
Working well, this is unremarkable: you look at what's actually in front of you, you pick, and you move. The picture of the finished thing can be satisfying before it's real, and that satisfaction is what pulls a choice forward instead of leaving it circling.

Where you are now, a direction got settled quietly and didn't get sent forward. You're steering something you won't admit you're steering, and the not-admitting is what's running the show. Say the decision to one person, and say what following it would require of you. Naming the requirement is how the direction becomes real again — not because the requirement is small, but because you stopped arguing with a decision already made.

cells.tense: You're steering this already, and you're talking about it like it's steering itself.
cells.ask: Write this sentence and finish it: "I've been calling this ___ when it's mine to pick." Then tell one person one thing you want from them in it.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing. You keep describing it as if it chose you.
cells.core:
Working right, this is a clear exchange: you say what you're picking, you say what you need from the people around you, and you can use what they hand back. The direction is shared because you named it, not because the people near you guessed.

What's happening now is the picking without the naming. You're already choosing — in what you say yes to, what you don't answer, what you quietly move toward — and it shows up as the way things happened to go. Write the sentence and finish it. Then tell one person one thing you want from them in it. Naming what you're steering and asking for what you need is how the choice becomes shared instead of ambient, and answers arrive when there's someone to answer.

attempts.check: The draft risks claiming the person is holding back something specific they already know — the record only says the knowing is present and undeclared, not what it is or why. A reader might reasonably say 'I'm not withholding anything, I just haven't decided yet,' which the card itself allows (it can look like indecision from outside). The asks all survive being wrong: writing down what you're actually steering and handing one line to someone teaches something either way. The sentence most likely to serve the writer is any line about the room being already written — it sounds true of everyone, so I've kept it to the seat's own image of steering and left what the person is deciding, and why, unspoken.

attempts.check: The draft still leans on two claims the record can't support: that the person already knows a specific thing they're withholding, and that there's a cost attached to acting on it. The card describes a capacity in a condition, not a biography — a reader could reasonably say 'I'm not hiding anything, I just don't know yet,' which the card itself allows as a reading. The asks survive being wrong because writing down what you're steering and saying one line to a person teaches something regardless. The sentences that most serve the writer are the ones about the room already being written and the wheel already being held — they flatter the reader; I've cut them to the seat's plain image of choosing and kept what is being decided, and why, off the page.
